profile.summary: CARP is a family of protein language models built from convolutions rather than attention. Each model reads an amino acid sequence and was pretrained to fill in masked residues, on the March 2020 release of UniRef50. It returns a representation for every residue, plus per-residue logits that can be used to score sequences. Because it is a convolutional network, cost grows linearly with length rather than quadratically.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Convolutional autoencoding representations of proteins (CARP); abstract

summary_quotes.text: We make available pretrained CNN protein sequence masked language models of various sizes. All of these have a ByteNet encoder architecture and are pretrained on the March 2020 release of UniRef50 using the same masked language modeling task as in BERT and ESM-1b.
convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures, which scale linearly with sequence length, could be as effective as transformers in protein language models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each CARP model is a ByteNet encoder: stacked convolutional layers with growing dilation, so a residue's representation takes in a widening window of neighbours without attention. In the paper, an embedding layer maps each token to 8 dimensions, a linear layer maps that to the model width, and a stack of ByteNet blocks with 1 x 5 dilated convolutions follows, with the dilation rate doubling each layer up to 128 and then restarting at 1; a final layer norm gives the representation and a linear decoder gives the logits. Pretraining selects 15% of residues, replaces 80% of them with a mask token, 10% with a random amino acid and leaves 10% unchanged, and asks the model to recover them, as in ESM-1b. The loader reads the width, depth, kernel size and dilation factor from the checkpoint and builds a ByteNetLM over the protein alphabet, then wraps it so padding is masked. Forward returns per-residue representations; with repr_layers and logits you also get intermediate layers and the vocabulary logits.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four sizes are released and are chosen by name in load_model_and_alphabet: carp_600k, carp_38M, carp_76M and carp_640M. The paper trained seven sizes, from CARP-4k to CARP-640M; The README lists only the four released names; CARP-4k, CARP-40k and CARP-24M are not among them. The loader fetches each released model from one Zenodo deposit, so a result should name the checkpoint and that deposit (record 6564798, dated 2022-03-18). The same loader also serves MIF, MIF-ST and BiGCARP from other deposits; MIF-ST pulls carp_640M in as its sequence model, so a MIF-ST result is not a CARP result.

quotes.text: We make available pretrained CNN protein sequence masked language models of various sizes.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: ByteNet encoder: stacked dilated convolutional layers with 1 x 5 kernels, dilation doubling up to 128 and repeating, then a final layer norm and a linear decoder. The loader builds a ByteNetLM with the embedding size, model width, layer count, kernel size and dilation factor stored in each checkpoint, with final layer normalisation and no causal masking. Per the paper's Table S1: CARP-600k 16 layers, d 128; CARP-38M 16 layers, d 1024; CARP-76M 32 layers, d 1024; CARP-640M 56 layers, d 1280.

facts.value: The cluster representatives of the March 2020 release of UniRef50: 41.5 million sequences for training, with about 83k held out for validation and 210k for testing. Masked language modelling as in ESM-1b. The Zenodo deposit also holds the uniref50 archive and splits used.

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: Four CARP checkpoints, loaded by name: carp_600k, carp_38M, carp_76M and carp_640M. The same repository also holds MIF, MIF-ST and three BiGCARP models, which are different models.

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: The pretraining data is the March 2020 release of UniRef50, so nothing later is in it. The date of the training run is not stated; the Zenodo deposit is dated 2022-03-18.

quotes.text: pretrained on the March 2020 release of UniRef50

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: No fixed limit: as a CNN it has no position embedding. CARP-640M was trained on sequences of at most 2048 residues, and the authors tested its pretraining loss up to 4096 residues, finding loss beyond 2048 comparable to that at 500 to 2048.

strengths.text: Cost grows linearly with sequence length. On a 48GB A100 the authors could run CARP-640M on sequences of 4096 residues and longer, while a same-size ESM-1b ran out of memory around 2048. They also scored mutations in Cas9, a 1368-residue protein that ESM-1b cannot take whole.

strengths.text: Four sizes from 600k to 640M, all loaded by one function call that downloads the weights.

run_guide.summary: Install the package, load a CARP checkpoint, and get per-residue representations for two short sequences.
prerequisites: PyTorch. The README says it was tested on 1.9.0, 1.11.0 and 1.12, and that pandas, scipy and wget may also be needed in a clean conda environment.
Internet access: the loader downloads the checkpoint from Zenodo on first use (2,572,014,451 bytes for carp_640M, 151,618,419 for carp_38M).
No GPU is required for the snippet; the bulk script uses one if present.

steps.title: Install
steps.explanation: The released package. The README also offers pip install git+https://github.com/microsoft/protein-sequence-models.git for the current main branch; that form cannot be pinned to a commit without changing the command.

steps.title: Load a checkpoint and encode two sequences
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from sequence_models.pretrained import load_model_and_alphabet

model, collater = load_model_and_alphabet('carp_640M')

seqs = [['MDREQ'], ['MGTRRLLP']]
x = collater(seqs)[0]  # (n, max_len)
rep = model(x)  # (n, max_len, d_model)
print(rep.shape)
PY
steps.explanation: The two README snippets joined in a shell heredoc, with a print added. The first call downloads carp_640M from Zenodo. Use carp_600k, carp_38M or carp_76M for a smaller model.
